title: Retail tenant SDK onboarding - auth, env and quickstart walkthrough
summary: AE+SE walkthrough of Redwood SDK quickstarts (Python + TS), environment auth patterns (API key, env var, SSO), local dev vs Dedicated, and initial POC next steps. Security asked about KMS/HSM + audit logs. Action items to share quickstart links and security pack, and schedule POC kickoff.
topics: API auth patterns: REDWOOD_API_KEY, SSO, service account tokens
Local dev env vs dedicated/private networking
Streaming and callback handling in Python/TS
Optimize suggestions: batching, cache, model choice
Security: KMS, audit logs, SOC2, data residency
transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-12-15 16:00 UTC | Duration: ~55m | Attendees: Lila, Roberto (Redwood); Olivia, Marcus, Priya, Samir (Nimbus)

[00:00] Lila: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Lila with Redwood Inference, and I have Roberto from SE to run through the SDK quickstart and auth flows.
[00:20] Olivia: Thanks, Lila. We want a quick hands-on: python + ts snippets, how to wire auth in CI, and what it looks like for Dedicated.
[00:35] Roberto: Great. I'll share my screen in a sec — showing our README and quickstart repo. We have a tiny pip package and an npm package, examples for python and typescript.
[01:05] Roberto: For python it's pip install redwood-inference (note: package name may vary, transcribed) then from redwood_inference import Client; client = Client(api_key=os.environ.get('REDWOOD_API_KEY'))
[01:30] Marcus: Is the env var name fixed? We want to standardize across services.
[01:40] Roberto: You can pick any var name in your code, but our docs use REDWOOD_API_KEY by convention. For CI we recommend storing the key in your secret manager and injecting at runtime. For Dedicated you can also mount a service account that renews tokens.
[02:10] Priya: How do you rotate keys and support KMS? We need HSM-backed keys for certain regs.
[02:25] Lila: We integrate with customer KMS for Private deployments and offer an option for HSM via our enterprise package; we also surface audit logs and API key rotation endpoints. We'll send the security pack after the call.
[03:00] Roberto: Back to the quickstart — TypeScript example: npm i @redwood-inference/sdk (again package name approximate) then import Redwood from '@redwood-inference/sdk'; const client = new Redwood({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY });
[03:30] Samir: Any built-in helpers for TypeScript types for responses?
[03:40] Roberto: Yes we ship types and helper parsers for streaming and function-like outputs; there's a typed chat client and generation client. We'll point to the exact repo.
[04:10] Roberto: Showing a live code sample — simple generation: client.generate({ model: 'redwood-2.1', prompt: 'Summarize sales data by region' }) — returns a streaming iterable you can await.
[04:45] Olivia: For streaming, will the SDK buffer or yield tokens as they come? We need low latency for UI.
[04:58] Roberto: The SDK yields tokens as they arrive; on python you get an async iterator, on TS you get event callbacks or async iterators depending on runtime. There's an option to aggregate per-chunk to balance event frequency vs render latency.
[05:30] Marcus: What about local dev proxying to a hosted instance, or mocking for offline dev?
[05:45] Roberto: We have a local CLI 'redwood dev-proxy' that proxies requests to hosted or to a local docker runtime for offline testing. It honors env flags like REDWOOD_ENV=dev and logs token counts locally.
[06:20] Priya: Does that leak data to your hosted control plane while developing? We need assurances for PII.
[06:32] Lila: Good callout. For dev-proxy you can run it entirely on-prem; the hosted control plane only sees metadata if you opt-in. For PII-sensitive flows we recommend Private deployment or Dedicated with VPC.
[07:05] Roberto: Now auth patterns: 1) Static API key (short lived recommended) 2) Service account token via OIDC 3) SSO for human users. For CI, service accounts with rotated tokens are best.
[07:40] Marcus: OIDC — can we mint tokens from our IAM and have Redwood accept them?
[07:50] Roberto: Yes, we support accepting JWTs from your IdP for Private deployments; we can map claims to RBAC roles. For Hosted, we support SSO and SCIM for provisioning; for Dedicated we do custom integrations.
[08:20] Olivia: Any sample code for token refresh in python?
[08:30] Roberto: There's a sample in the repo. Example: client = Client(token_provider=MyTokenProvider()) where MyTokenProvider implements get_token() and refresh_token() — the SDK will call it when a 401 happens.
[09:10] Speaker 2: (mumble) I'm seeing a snippet in the chat — copy link?
[09:20] Roberto: Pasted the quickstart link: https://redwood.ai/examples/sdk-quickstart (transcribed link may be wrong) and security pack: drive.google.com/XXX (placeholder).
[09:45] Samir: On models — what variants do you recommend for retail product copy vs embedding catalog items?
[09:58] Roberto: For embeddings we have specialized embedding models; for short-form product copy a small/medium generation model is cheaper and faster. For retrieval-augmented generation, use embeddings + reranker. Optimize will suggest batching/quantization profiles based on token distribution.
[10:40] Olivia: Show us the Optimize suggestions?
[10:50] Roberto: Quick tour of Console -> Optimize: you upload a sample prompt set or connect telemetry; it suggests batching windows, prefix caching for common prompts, and whether a quantized int8 path is ok. There's also a cost delta estimate.
[11:30] Lila: Important note: Optimize's suggestions are workload-specific; for very low latency (<50ms) you might reduce batching. For throughput use larger batch and consider Dedicated.
[12:00] Marcus: For our nightly catalog embedding job (large throughput), can we run that on Dedicated and route user-facing calls to Hosted?
[12:15] Roberto: Yes — smart routing can route by policy to Dedicated for heavy batch jobs and hosted for bursty user traffic. Also can fallback if capacity low.
[12:45] Priya: A few security questions: where are logs stored, retention, and can we export to our SIEM?
[12:58] Lila: Audit logs are available and can be exported to your S3 or pushed to your SIEM via webhook/syslog. Retention is configurable on Dedicated and Private. We'll include retention options in the security doc.
[13:30] Olivia: Back on SDK: debugging — are there verbose request traces?
[13:45] Roberto: There's an env flag REDWOOD_DEBUG=1 that emits request/response tracing locally; on Console you have per-request tracing and token-level latency in the Observability tab.
[14:15] Roberto: Now a short live-coding: Python dev flow — create venv, pip install redwood-inference, export REDWOOD_API_KEY, run example/generate.py. I'll paste the file:
[14:40] [code readout] # example/generate.py
[14:43] import os
[14:45] from redwood_inference import Client
[14:47] client = Client(api_key=os.environ.get('REDWOOD_API_KEY'))
[14:50] resp = client.generate(model='redwood-2.1', prompt='List top 5 seasonal items by revenue')
[14:56] print('
'.join(resp.stream()))
[15:10] Olivia: That stream() API — is stream() synchronous? We have async worker fleet.
[15:20] Roberto: We have both sync and async variants; stream() in the example is sync for simplicity, but there is an async_stream() on the client for asyncio.
[15:50] Marcus: For TypeScript callbacks — does the SDK integrate with our React front end easily? WebSocket or SSE?
[16:05] Roberto: We support SSE for browser-safe streaming and WebSocket for lower-latency server-to-server. The TS SDK has a small browser bundle that does SSE polyfills.
[16:35] Samir: Any CORS concerns?
[16:40] Roberto: If you call from browser you'll need to use a short-lived token minted from your backend; we recommend never embedding long-lived API keys in frontend code.
[17:10] Priya: About data residency — our EU customers' PII must stay in EU. Can you pin region?
[17:22] Lila: Yes, you can pin region on both Hosted and Dedicated; Private gives full control. We'll include region options.
[17:50] Roberto: Quick note on cost controls — you can set per-route rate limits, per-key quotas and enforce fallback to smaller model to cap spend.
[18:15] Olivia: For the POC we want: 1) small integration with python service, 2) embedding batch job, 3) a UI demo with streaming. Timeline: 4 weeks ideally.
[18:35] Lila: That aligns — typical POC is 3-6 weeks. We'll scope success criteria and SLOs.
[19:00] Roberto: I'll run through a short demo of streaming code in TS — showing an async iterator, error handling for 429 and 503 and automatic retry/backoff policies in SDK.
[19:30] Roberto: For retries, SDK respects Retry-After and we have configurable backoff with jitter. For rate-limits we expose headers X-RateLimit-Remaining and recommend client-side throttling.
[20:05] Samir: Can we run an end-to-end benchmark? We want latency p50/p95 numbers hitting our UI flow.
[20:17] Lila: Yes — next steps include a small benchmark script. We can run it against Hosted or a Dedicated eval cluster. We'll run sample queries and share a spreadsheet.
[20:45] Priya: On compliance, do you have SOC2 or ISO?
[20:55] Lila: We are SOC 2 compliant and pursuing ISO 27001; security pack includes attestation and our compliance timeline.
[21:30] Roberto: Now a quick show of Optimize in the Console. Walkthrough: upload prompts -> get batching + quantization recommendations -> estimated cost savings. Example suggestion: enable prefix caching for catalog prompts (saves 20% tokens).
[22:05] Marcus: How do we feed telemetry? With a small SDK hook or via logs?
[22:15] Roberto: You can forward request metadata to Optimize via our ingestion API or enable telemetry collection on the SDK which anonymizes content by default.
[22:45] Olivia: We need to know the impact on accuracy if you quantize to int8.
[22:55] Roberto: Optimize runs a small set of eval prompts against quantized variants and shows quality delta. For critical prompts we recommend a manual review set to validate.
[23:30] Lila: Quick pause — any blockers for proceeding to a POC?
[23:38] Olivia: Main blockers: security sign-off (Priya), and exact cost estimate to attach to our budget.
[24:00] Priya: We'll need a data flow diagram and answers on retention and access controls.
[24:12] Lila: We'll include a runbook and data flow diagram in the security packet.
[24:35] Roberto: Back to code, error handling patterns: detect 401 -> rotate token; 429 -> backoff; 5xx -> local retries then fallback to smaller model or cached response.
[25:00] Samir: Is there built-in reranker or do we need to host our own?
[25:10] Roberto: We have a reranker endpoint and SDK helper to score candidates, common for retrieval pipelines.
[25:40] Olivia: For embeddings throughput, we want a bulk upload API.
[25:50] Roberto: We support batch embedding endpoints and streaming ingest for very large corpora; there's also tooling to checkpoint progress.
[26:15] Marcus: Let's talk about networking for Dedicated — do you support private peering or VPC peering?
[26:30] Lila: Dedicated supports VPC peering and Private offers on-prem connectors. For strict networks we deploy an appliance or use site-to-site.
[27:05] Priya: Audit question: can we restrict which roles can call generation vs embeddings?
[27:15] Roberto: Yes, RBAC can be enforced by route/model; roles scoped via claims mapping.
[27:40] Olivia: Any latency numbers for redwood-2.1 on a 16k seq?
[27:50] Roberto: Latency depends on deployment/quantization; roughly p50 80-120ms for short contexts, larger seqs scale linearly; we'll share benchmark docs.
[28:15] Samir: How do we handle model rollouts? Can we do A/B?
[28:25] Roberto: Console supports canary, A/B, percentage rollouts per-route. You pin versions and set fallback models.
[29:00] Lila: Ok we'll recap next steps in chat.
[29:08] Roberto: I'll paste links to sample repos, the quickstart, security pack, and a blank POC checklist.
[29:30] Olivia: Great. Quick Q: is there a usage-based invoice or committed usage for POC?
[29:40] Lila: For POC we often do usage credits; for Dedicated we discuss reserved capacity.
[30:05] [15m silence while links are pasted and people scan]
[45:10] Marcus: We looked at the TS example — small comment about bundling polyfills for SSE. We'll test in our staging environment.
[45:30] Roberto: Noted. I'll add an explicit note about SSE polyfills for React SSR.
[46:00] Priya: We'll review the security doc and come back with a list of questions; prefer a follow-up technical deep-dive with infra team.
[46:20] Lila: Sounds good. Proposed dates? Next week Thu/Mon?
[46:30] Samir: Monday works for us.
[46:40] Lila: Great. Recap — we'll send quickstart links, security pack, sample benchmark script, and propose POC kickoff for 2025-12-22.
[46:55] Olivia: Thanks. One last minor thing — what's the best practice for logging prompts vs hashed tokens?
[47:05] Roberto: We recommend hashing/scrubbing prompts before shipping telemetry, and Optimize anonymizes by default. We'll include examples.
[47:30] Lila: Any final Qs?
[47:40] Priya: None from me.
[47:45] Olivia: All good. Thanks for the walkthrough.
[47:50] Lila: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with materials and next steps.
[47:58] Meeting end.

Notes on transcription: occasional transcription errors in package names and links are expected; links in chat are placeholders.
